Include work and school hours, travel, sleep, shared walls, other pets, available space and who will take responsibility for daily care. The most attractive bird is not necessarily the bird whose routine you can sustain. A parrot may be noisy, destructive of suitable materials, wary of change or uninterested in talking; make a plan that remains workable in those ordinary moments.

paragraph_excerpt: There is no single paperwork rule for every parrot. The scientific name, lawful origin, proposed transaction, housing arrangements and journey all matter. Use this guide to prepare questions, not to certify an individual bird.

There is no single document set that applies to every parrot in the UK. Requirements can turn on the exact species and scientific name, where the specimen originated, whether the use is commercial, the bird’s identification, and whether it will stay in one jurisdiction or cross a border. This guide is a practical prompt for checking those facts, not a legal determination that any individual bird may be sold, kept or moved.

For a proposed transaction, identify the actual bird and the proposed activity before relying on a seller’s summary. Ask for copies of relevant records, compare identity details and dates, and establish who is responsible for any required original certificate or permit. If anything is uncertain, contact the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), the relevant UK administration or the destination authority before payment, contract or transport arrangements.

paragraph_excerpt: The Sun Conure is a vivid, medium-small South American parrot with yellow, orange and green plumage. It is often highly social and energetic, but its piercing calls and need for engagement deserve serious thought before choosing one.

Sun Conures are known for bright yellow and orange plumage, green wing feathers and a long tapered tail. Young birds can show more green, with colour developing as they mature. They are native to northern South America and are active, social parrots rather than quiet cage birds.

Their brilliant colouring can draw attention, but suitability depends on ordinary daily realities: noise, interaction, exercise and long-term care. Provide safe opportunities to climb, investigate and forage, and allow the bird to retreat from activity when it chooses.

paragraph_excerpt: The Papuan Eclectus is a striking parrot from the New Guinea region, notable for vivid colour differences between males and females. Their plumage does not predict temperament: individuals need careful observation, a balanced routine and a considered nutrition plan.

Papuan Eclectus Parrots show pronounced sexual dimorphism: adult males are predominantly green with orange on the bill, while females are chiefly red and purple with a dark bill. Current classifications distinguish the Papuan Eclectus, Eclectus polychloros, from the Moluccan Eclectus, Eclectus roratus. Older references may use the latter name for a broader Eclectus complex.

Papuan Eclectus Parrots occur in New Guinea and nearby areas, with geographic variation. Their distinctive colour is a biological difference, not a guide to a bird’s character, trainability or suitability. Verify the identity and background of an individual with reliable records where relevant.

Native to parts of Central and South America, wild birds use large areas and remain active in social settings. A companion needs comparable opportunities to climb, manipulate objects and make choices. Their spectacular appearance should never distract from the extensive daily and long-term commitment.

Scarlet Macaws have vivid red body plumage, broad yellow and blue sections on the wings and a long tapered tail. Their bare facial skin has fine feather lines. They are large birds with a strong hooked bill, capable feet and substantial movement needs; proportions and colour can vary with age and individual.

In the wild they inhabit forests and other wooded landscapes in Central and South America. Their social lives and wide-ranging activity are a useful reminder that a companion Scarlet Macaw needs meaningful daily choices and stimulation, not just a visually impressive enclosure.

paragraph_excerpt: The Budgerigar is a small Australian parakeet with a long tail, lively flock behaviour and an unexpectedly rich capacity for learning. Its modest size still calls for flight, companionship, suitable nutrition and daily enrichment.

Budgerigars are small, slender parakeets with a long tail and fine barring across the head and wings. Wild-type birds are green and yellow, while selective breeding has produced many colour varieties. The cere above the beak can help with sex identification, but appearance can be less clear in young birds and some colour forms.

Native to Australia, budgies are naturally social and active. They use flight, calls and close observation to interact with their surroundings. Captive birds need room to move, opportunities to forage and a safe social environment; their small size does not make companionship optional.

paragraph_excerpt: The Indian Ringneck is a long-tailed, medium-sized parakeet known for its alert nature and potential to learn sounds. It needs patient socialisation, regular flight and enrichment, and should not be chosen on assumptions about speech or tameness.

Indian Ringnecks have a slender body, long pointed tail and strong red bill. Green is common in the wild-type form, and captive colour varieties are widely seen. Adult males typically develop a dark and rose-coloured neck ring; females and young birds may not show the same markings. Colour varieties and age can make visual sex identification uncertain.

The species belongs to the rose-ringed parakeet group and is native across parts of Africa and South Asia. Its nimble flight and active exploratory behaviour mean a home needs safe movement space as well as an enclosure.

Peach-faced Lovebirds have a green body, peach-pink face and chest, and a short, rounded tail. Captive colour mutations can produce other combinations, but the species is identified by its compact form and characteristic face in the wild-type bird. It is native to south-western Africa.

Despite their small size, lovebirds are active parrots with strong bills and clear preferences. They need more than a tiny cage and a mirror: safe flight, social contact and opportunities to forage and chew are central to daily life.
